What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2026
Californians and Their GovernmentOctober 2026
Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

content.thinking:
Emerson apparently didn't poll Prop 2. The broader climate looks strongly Democratic, with Becerra ahead by roughly 24 to 27 points and Trump's approval in California around 26 to 33 percent, which tends to help Democratic-backed measures like Prop 2. I'm also going to check the California Today guide for ballot return data, since if Democrats are leading early returns that would be another point in Prop 2's favor.

I'm now going to check the PPIC October crosstabs for how Prop 2 support breaks down among people who have already voted, and I'll pull the likely voter crosstabs PDF to do it.

Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

I'm settling on the column order now: SF Bay Area, Orange/San Diego, Los Angeles, Inland Empire, Central Valley, then Con, Mod, Lib, Ind, Rep, Dem, and the total last. The header got scrambled in extraction, so I'm checking the unweighted n values to confirm where each one belongs.

So Prop 2 breaks down by region as SF Bay Area at 67%, Orange/San Diego at 58%, Los Angeles at 66%, Inland Empire at 58%, and Central Valley at 54%, with every region above 50% yes. Now I'm moving on to the other demographic block, where the yes figures run from 52% to 77% across the sub-groups.

I'm now checking the second demographic block against the unweighted counts, since the header order is scrambled. I'm now looking at the age and gender groups in the second block, where the yes figures seem to run from 53% for 55+ up to 77% for 18-34. Latinos, whites, and other groups fall in the middle, and the men and women values look close to each other. The 55+ result is still a majority, though that group carries a lot of weight in a midterm electorate.

I'm matching the income and education numbers to their groups by pairing the values so each set sums to the sample total. The first pair is renters and owners, then naturalized and native-born, then the three income brackets, and last the three education levels.

I'm reading the rest of the demographic values in this block, where the group yes figures come out to 74% for renters, 57% for owners, 65% for naturalized citizens, 60% for native-born, and 60%, 61%, and 74% across the three income brackets. Education is last, with 69% for college graduates, 50% for those with some college, and 61% for high school only. Some college is the weakest group at 50%, and every other group is above that.

Now I'm checking whether any late campaign activity or news in the final days could shift the Prop 2 numbers, since the poll has been stable at 60 to 61 percent yes.

# Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).

## Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.

Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to
- Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
- Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
- Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

PROP 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%202.pdf)

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

PROP 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%202.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

I've got enough to go on. Prop 2 on the November 3, 2026 ballot would grow the State's Rainy Day Fund through a legislative constitutional amendment that needs only a simple majority to pass. Both PPIC polls show it ahead, 60-39 in September and 61-38 in October, with a majority across every region and group, and I'm not finding any other polling. No funded campaign has registered on either side yet, and I'm now looking at who has come out in support, starting with Newsom.

I'm going through the rest of the support and opposition, including the editorial boards on each side. The prediction markets sit around 82% for Yes, and the historical comparisons and the Democratic-leaning midterm environment point the same way.

assistantMessageEvent.delta: ority support in every region and every dem

assistantMessageEvent.content:
yes

I'm confident in this. Results weren't posted when I checked (election night is November 3, 2026), so this is a forecast.

- **Polling:** The Public Policy Institute of California, the only pollster that asked about Prop 2, had it at 60% yes to 39% no in September and 61% to 38% in October. In October it had majority support in every region and every demographic group. Republicans were opposed, 23% yes, but Democrats were at 85% and independents at 57%. This pollster's October numbers have usually landed within about 5 points of the final result, so Prop 2 would need an unusually large late collapse to fail.
- **No real opposition campaign:** As of October 22, the Secretary of State listed no campaign committee for or against Prop 2. Opposition came from the Republican Party, Carl DeMaio's Reform California, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which called it a "Band-Aid," and a few editorial boards. None of them funded a "No" campaign, so most voters will mainly see the friendly ballot title, "Increases State's Rainy Day Fund."
- **Support:** Newsom, Becerra and the state Democratic Party back it, along with firefighters, hospitals, the LA Chamber of Commerce and the state PTA. The SF Chronicle, Mercury News and Sacramento Bee editorial boards endorsed it. The midterm looks Democratic-leaning, with Becerra up 24 to 27 points.
- **History:** Earlier rainy-day fund measures passed easily: 71% in 2004 and 69% in 2014.
- **Betting markets:** On November 2, Kalshi gave it a 92% chance of passing and Polymarket about 72%, though very little money was being traded.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Press Release · October 27, 2026
Californians Head to Polls in Historically Sour Mood; Billionaire Wealth Tax Slips below Majority Support
BECERRA PRESERVES WIDE LEAD OVER HILTON; ENTHUSIASM GAP FAVORS DEMOCRATS IN CONGRESSIONAL RACES; SOLID MAJORITY FAVOR HIGH-EARNER INCOME TAX MEASURE
Full survey report → (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/)
Comunicado de prensa (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/1026-mbs-spanish.pdf)
Related Event
Statewide Survey: Californians and Their Government · October 28, 2026 (https://www.ppic.org/event/statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/)
Contact
Matt Levin
Director of Digital Strategy
[email protected] (https://www.ppic.org/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#a9c4cccdc0c8e9d9d9c0ca87c6dbce)
916-440-1124 (tel:916-440-1124)
SAN FRANCISCO, October 27, 2026—A week ahead of Election Day, Californians are exceptionally pessimistic about the direction of the country, the state, and the economy. Support for a high-profile initiative that would tax billionaires appears to be eroding. Democrat Xavier Becerra maintains a commanding lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race for governor. And Democrats are far more excited than Republicans or independents about voting in congressional races. These are among the key findings from a statewide survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Eighty-two percent of adult Californians think things in the United States are generally going in the wrong direction, the highest share holding this pessimistic view since PPIC began asking about the national outlook two decades ago. Nearly eight in ten predict bad economic conditions in both the state and the nation over the next 12 months, a high not matched since the depths of the pandemic and Great Recession.
“If you’re looking for one word to describe Californians’ mood as they are filling out their ballots, it would be gloomy—very gloomy,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC Statewide Survey director and Miller Chair in Public Policy. “Affordability continues to be a central concern, with majorities across demographic groups saying their incomes are not keeping up with inflation.”
In the race for governor, Democrat Xavier Becerra has a 24 point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (61% to 37%), including a 13 point lead among independent likely voters. Californians say they are largely satisfied with their choices for governor, although that satisfaction appears to vary significantly by age: while nearly 70 percent of likely voters 55 and older are pleased with their gubernatorial choices, only half of younger voters aged 18 to 34 are satisfied.
More key findings from the survey:
Billionaire wealth tax falls below majority support: Forty-six percent of likely voters say they will vote yes on Proposition 40, a controversial citizens’ initiative that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5 percent on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. Last month, 52 percent of likely voters said they would support the measure.
“Since last month, we’ve seen declining support for Prop 40, particularly among Democrats and independents,” said Baldassare. “Propositions 41 and 42, which could effectively nullify Prop 40 even if it was passed, are now polling better than the billionaire tax.”
While support for the billionaire wealth tax appears to be eroding, a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would make a temporary marginal income tax on high earners permanent. Among Democrats, 80 percent support Proposition 3, while 64 percent support the billionaire wealth tax.
Enthusiasm gap favors Democrats in congressional races: Seventy-one percent of Democratic likely voters say they are more enthusiastic than usual about voting in congressional elections, compared to 46 percent of Republicans. The partisan enthusiasm gap is larger than it was ahead of the 2024 general election.
Unhappiness with the Trump administration is likely playing a role. Seventy-eight percent of California adults disapprove of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president—the president’s highest disapproval rating among Californians during his two terms in office. Since the beginning of the year, the president’s approval ratings have dropped most acutely among independents, from 25 percent in February to 16 percent in October.
Majorities back bond measures, oppose tax restrictions: Majorities of California likely voters back the three borrowing measures on the November ballot. More than 60 percent support Propositions 1 and 37, which would authorize tens of billions in bonds for housing programs. Fifty-seven percent say they will vote yes on Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology research. A majority also support Proposition 2, which increases the amount of revenue the state can deposit into a rainy day fund.
A majority of likely voters oppose Proposition 43, which would make it more difficult to increase local taxes. A slim majority oppose Proposition 45 (50% oppose, 46% approve), which would modify the state’s marquee environmental law to speed construction of some new developments.
Californians are skeptical about the need for voter ID: Nearly 60 percent of likely voters oppose Proposition 39, a citizens’ initiative that would require government-issued ID at the polls. Despite federal allegations of rampant voter fraud, 63 percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
About the Survey
The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The findings are based on responses from 1,728 California adult residents. The sampling error is ±3.0 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample and ±3.8 percent for the 1,086 likely voters. Interviewing took place from October 16–22, 2026. For more information, please see the methodology section in the full survey report.
Mark Baldassare is statewide survey director at PPIC, where he holds the Arjay and Frances Fearing Miller Chair in Public Policy. He is founder of the PPIC Statewide Survey, which he has directed since 1998.
The Public Policy Institute of California is dedicated to informing and improving public policy in California through independent, objective, nonpartisan research. We are a public charity. We do not take or support positions on any ballot measure or on any local, state, or federal legislation, nor do we endorse, support, or oppose any political parties or candidates for public office. Research publications reflect the views of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of our funders or of the staff, officers, advisory councils, or board of directors of the Public Policy Institute of California.

## Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.

## What Prop. 2 Would Do
Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to
- Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
- Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
- Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.
- Clarify the account’s interaction with state constitutional limits on appropriations (setting funds aside for a specific purpose).

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. 1. California Prop 2 2026: Larger state rainy day fund
https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-02
# Proposition 2 : Larger state rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high.
It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.
...

The idea was to transfer a certain percentage of general fund revenue to these accounts, which could only be drawn down in a state emergency.
The BSA is essentially the state's rainy day fund, which would be used to avoid tax increases during recessionary periods.
The state controller annually transfers 1.5% of estimated general fund revenues to the BSA each fiscal year.
