California has more revenue than expected thanks to AI. Should the state save it?
By
Yue Stella Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)
Published October 23, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT
Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it&display=page)
WhatsApp (https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it)
Email (mailto:?body=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it%0A%0AProponents%20say%20Prop.%202%20would%20allow%20the%20state%20to%20shore%20up%20its%20reserves%20for%20an%20economic%20downturn.%20Critics%20say%20it%20would%20only%20allow%20state%20leaders%20to%20spend%20more%20in%20the%20future.)
Fred Greaves
/
CalMatters
Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025.
This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/) . Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.
“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we're here for fiscal responsibility, it's like the devil offering a Bible study. Don't buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

I've confirmed the main facts from the KPBS and CalMatters coverage: little funded opposition, polls around 60 to 61 percent yes, and the HJTA and Reform California opposing it. Next I'm weighing whether voter fatigue from the 14 propositions could push people toward "No" on the measures they know least about.

I'm weighing whether the fiscal-prudence amendments have historically passed easily, as Prop 2 and Prop 58 did, while noting that Prop 1A failed amid an anti-government mood. I'm also checking the PPIC poll at 61-38, expecting support to erode somewhat, and wondering whether other polls or a funded No campaign might change the picture.

I'm trying to recall how PPIC and other pollsters tracked the 2024 propositions, like Prop 6 and Prop 33, to judge whether polls in this race are reliable. I'm also checking whether Prop 2 passed with more or less support than the early polls suggested.

I'm comparing PPIC's past October polls against actual results for several propositions, where the early yes numbers ran a few points above what voters delivered. At 61 percent, I'd expect Prop 2 to land somewhere around 55 to 60 percent.

I'm checking whether other polls exist beyond PPIC, since Berkeley IGS apparently skipped Prop 2 in September. I'm also wondering whether the Republican Party or Libertarian Party have taken official positions, and whether any funded No campaign has formed.

California Prop 2 guide: Expanded "Rainy Day Fund" would double amount saved for state budget reserves
Proposition 2 doubles the cap on California's rainy day fund to 20% of General Fund taxes, sets aside more of a capital gains surge, extends required debt payments to 2040 and stops counting deposits against the Gann spending limit until withdrawn.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 19, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Rainy Day Fund is going before voters as Proposition 2, which would let the state save up to 20% of its General Fund taxes for downturns.
Proposition 2 would double the cap on California's rainy day fund, the reserve the state draws on when a recession or stock market slump cuts tax revenue. Today the state must keep saving until the fund holds 10% of General Fund taxes.
Prop 2 raises that ceiling to 20%, requires larger deposits in years when capital gains revenue surges, and keeps the state making extra payments on its debts through 2040 instead of 2030. It also changes how savings count against the state's voter-approved spending limit, known as the Gann limit: deposits would no longer count when they are made, only when the money is taken out. The measure raises no taxes and spends no money. The Legislative Analyst's Office sums up its fiscal effect in six words: "State budget reserves would be higher."
California's Rainy Day Fund is capturing more of a capital gains surge under Proposition 2, which counts revenue above 10% of General Fund taxes at 150%. Prop 2, the Save for California's Future Act, is a legislative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/) that the Legislature placed on the ballot as ACA 20, by Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, on June 25. It rewrites the rules voters adopted in 2014, also as Proposition 2, and is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). PPIC's September survey found 60% of likely voters in favor and 39% opposed, one of the strongest results on the ballot. No campaign committee has registered on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, how the fund has been used since 2014, the spending-limit fight at the center of the opposition, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 2 doubles the cap on California's rainy day fund to 20% of General Fund taxes:
The rainy day fund's formal name is the Budget Stabilization Account. Voters created it in 2004 with Proposition 58 and gave it its current rules in 2014. Under those rules, the state sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues every year. Through 2029–30, half goes into the rainy day fund and half goes to paying down debts. The state must also set aside capital gains tax revenue above a threshold in boom years, split the same way. Once the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes, required deposits stop and the money that would have gone in must be spent on infrastructure.
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article XVI, sections 20 and 22 of the California Constitution. Its central change is one number: the cap on required deposits rises from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes. In its April 2025 report on the state's reserves, the Legislative Analyst's Office (https://www.lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) put the 10% cap at "about $21 billion." At that level of revenue, a 20% cap would be about $42 billion. The new rules apply from the 2027–28 fiscal year, and the money already in the fund stays there.
The 1.5% annual set-aside does not change. Neither do the rules for getting money out. The Governor still has to declare a budget emergency before deposits can be suspended or money withdrawn, and no more than half the fund can be withdrawn in a year unless money was also withdrawn the year before. The measure also says it does not change the minimum funding guarantee for schools under Proposition 98, and the separate school reserve keeps its own rules.
California's rainy day fund rules today and under Proposition 2 compared:

Cap on required rainy day fund savings 10% of General Fund taxes. Required deposits above the cap must go to infrastructure. 20% of General Fund taxes. Required deposits above the cap still go to infrastructure.

content.text:
The Governor issues a proclamation, which is required before deposits can be suspended or money withdrawn A May Revision that proposes a suspension or withdrawal counts as the proclamation, when the conditions for a budget emergency exist
Withdrawal limits No more than half the balance in a fiscal year, unless money was also withdrawn the year before Unchanged

Compiled by California Today from the text of Proposition 2 (ACA 20, Resolution Chapter 130 of 2026), the Legislative Analyst's analysis and the Assembly floor analysis of ACA 20 (June 22, 2026). The new rules apply from the 2027–28 fiscal year; money already in the rainy day fund stays there.
Proposition 2 would set aside 150% of capital gains revenue above 10% of General Fund taxes:
California's income tax leans on high earners, whose income often includes gains from selling stock, so state revenue rises and falls with the market. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm) notes that in a bad recession or market crash, revenue declines over a few years "can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues." The capital gains rule is the part of the rainy day fund meant to catch a boom before it is spent. Proposition 3 on the same ballot, which would make the current high-earner income tax rates (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-millionaire-tax-proposition-3/) permanent, concerns the same high-income tax base.
Today, when capital gains tax revenue exceeds 8% of General Fund taxes, the amount above 8% is set aside dollar for dollar, after subtracting the share that goes to schools under Proposition 98. Prop 2 splits that excess into two tiers. Revenue between 8% and 10% of General Fund taxes is still set aside dollar for dollar. Revenue above 10% is counted at 150%, so a $1 billion surge above that line requires a $1.5 billion set-aside. Through 2039–40, half of each year's total still goes to the rainy day fund and half to debts.
The Department of Finance estimated that if the new rule had applied from 2019–20 through 2021–22, the pandemic-era stock boom, about $4.7 billion more would have gone into the rainy day fund, according to the Assembly's floor analysis of ACA 20 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/media/8124). Looking back further, the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/), a nonpartisan research group that takes no position on ballot measures, found the change would have required extra set-asides in six of the 14 years from 2010–11 through 2023–24.
Required debt payments under Proposition 2 would run through 2040 and cover federal unemployment loans:
The half of the annual set-aside that goes to debts has been restricted to a short list since 2014: pension and retiree health debts, school funding the state owed as of July 1, 2014, budget loans outstanding on January 1, 2014, and old claims from local governments for state-mandated costs. The requirement ends after 2029–30. After that, the Legislature could put the money into the rainy day fund instead.
Prop 2 keeps the requirement through 2039–40 and widens the list. It drops the 2014 cutoffs for school funding owed and for budget loans between state funds. It allows early payment of two costs the state has scheduled for later years: loans to a Medi-Cal provider payment fund and a school funding obligation under Education Code section 41206.04. It also adds federal loans to the state's Unemployment Fund. California has borrowed from the federal government to pay unemployment benefits since 2020, and the Employment Development Department projects (https://edd.ca.gov/siteassets/files/unemployment/pdf/january-2026-ui-fund-forecast.pdf) that balance at $22.1 billion by the end of 2026. Any money set aside for debts beyond what the listed debts need would go into the rainy day fund.
The Budget Center questions the unemployment addition. It says the debt is an employer cost and that paying it from the General Fund shifts that cost to the state without fixing how the unemployment fund is financed.
Rainy day fund deposits would stop counting toward the state appropriations limit under Proposition 2:
The state appropriations limit, adopted by voters in 1979 and often called the Gann limit after its sponsor Paul Gann, caps how much tax revenue the state can spend each year. Its purpose, as the Senate Budget Committee describes it, is to keep inflation-adjusted spending per person under 1978–79 levels. Money put into reserves counts against the limit in the year it is deposited, just as spending does. If revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years, the excess is split between schools and taxpayer rebates. The state has issued a rebate once: in 1986–87 it exceeded the limit and returned $1.1 billion to taxpayers, according to an LAO history (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3596) of the limit.
Prop 2 changes when savings count. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count against the limit when they are made. They would count in the year the money is withdrawn and spent. The measure gives the same treatment to the state's temporary surplus holding account, a statutory account where the state parks revenue that may not last, up to 10% of General Fund taxes in a year. The state put $6.4 billion into that account for 2026–27, according to the LAO's overview (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5197) of the budget, which says neither it nor the Department of Finance treats the account as a reserve.
The practical effect is that in a boom year, when the state is most likely to be near the limit, saving would no longer use up room under it. The Budget Center estimates the change could add up to a few billion dollars of room in some years. The state is not near the limit now: the LAO puts the 2026–27 budget $27.3 billion below it.
This is the change opponents focus on. They argue that taking deposits out of the calculation lets the state collect revenue it would otherwise have to refund. Supporters argue that the current rule penalizes saving. The Department of Finance said in 2025 that the interaction between the 10% cap and the spending limit had kept the state from saving more during upswings, according to the Senate Budget Committee's February 2026 hearing agenda (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/media/3464) on reserves. A separate measure on the same ballot, Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/), also concerns the spending limit, but it targets new taxes whose revenue is excluded from the limit rather than reserve deposits. It is one of the two countermeasures to the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/).
Proposition 2 would let the Governor's May Revision count as a budget emergency proclamation:
Under current rules, deposits can be suspended or money withdrawn only after the Governor proclaims a budget emergency. That requires either a disaster or a finding that available money falls short of the highest spending level in the last three budgets, adjusted for inflation and population. Prop 2 adds a new subdivision (c) to section 22. When those conditions exist, the Governor's May Revision of the budget would itself count as the proclamation if it proposes suspending a deposit or withdrawing money. The Budget Center notes that in 2025 the Governor issued a separate proclamation on June 27, after the Legislature had passed the budget. The definition of a budget emergency does not change.
California's rainy day fund peaked near $23 billion and holds $15.1 billion after two years of withdrawals:
The 2014 Proposition 2 passed with 69.1% of the vote, according to the Secretary of State's Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2014-general/pdf/06-summary.pdf). The fund was first tapped in 2020–21, when the pandemic opened a budget gap, and then rebuilt with the revenue boom that followed. The 10% cap was operative in only two years, 2022–23 and 2023–24, and the LAO estimates that without it the state would have deposited about $2 billion more. The fund peaked at about $23 billion.
The state then drew it down. Over 2024–25 and 2025–26, it withdrew about $12.2 billion and suspended deposits in both years, according to the Senate Budget Committee. The LAO's figures show the balance at $18.6 billion at the end of 2024–25 and $11.5 billion at the end of 2025–26. The 2026–27 budget suspended a further $5.4 billion deposit owed for 2025–26, on top of a $1.6 billion deposit already suspended for that year, and ends 2026–27 with $15.1 billion in the fund. The Legislature passed ACA 20 on June 25 and the budget was chaptered on June 29, according to the Senate Republican Caucus office's summary (https://src.senate.ca.gov/content/2026-27-enacted-budget-initial-summary) of the enacted budget. Counting the Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties, the state's other general reserve, the LAO puts reserves available for any program at about $20 billion. The school reserve under Proposition 98 holds another $9.2 billion.
Legislative Analyst's Office recommended a 50% rainy day fund cap by 2055; Proposition 2 sets 20%:
Raising the cap has been on the table since early 2025. Governor Gavin Newsom's January 2025 budget proposed a 20% cap and taking deposits out of the spending limit, which is the core of Prop 2. The Legislature's own 2025 budget plan floated a 25% cap. Neither passed that year.
The LAO's April 2025 report modeled how often reserves would cover the gap between revenue and spending in future downturns. It found that the current rules would cover about one-third of funding shortfalls over 50 years and that the Governor's 2025 version would cover about half. It recommended going further: a cap phased up to 50% of General Fund taxes by 2055, starting at 20% "immediately after the next statewide election," then 25% in 2030 and 5 more points every five years, along with larger deposit rules. Prop 2 adopts the first step and a stronger capital gains rule. It does not schedule further increases.
Proposition 2 has no campaign committee on either side:
The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-2-aca-20-gabriel-save-californias-future-act-res-ch-130-2026) lists "No committees identified as of 10/06/2026" in support or in opposition, and Prop 2 does not appear on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), last updated October 14. The Voter Information Guide lists a Yes on Prop. 2 campaign in Los Angeles and names Assemblymember David Tangipa as the contact for the opposition.
The arguments on Proposition 2 split over savings and taxpayer rebates:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Darrell Roberts of the California Professional Firefighters, Assemblymember Gabriel and Maria S. Salinas of the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, says the state's economy "swung our state budget from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years." It says Prop 2 will "DOUBLE THE STATE'S RESERVE REQUIREMENT" and "STOP SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING" by requiring the state "to bank more of that windfall instead of committing it to new ongoing spending." It points out that the LAO "has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require." Its rebuttal, signed by State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, California Hospital Association CEO Carmela Coyle and California Primary Care Association CEO Francisco J. Silva, calls the rebate opponents describe "theoretical" and says it "relies on a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving."
The argument against, signed by Assemblymember Tangipa, vice chair of the Assembly Budget Committee, Senator Steven Choi and Assemblymember Carl DeMaio of Reform California, says Prop. 2 "allows the politicians to gut the voter-imposed spending limit." It calls the fund "a SLUSH FUND" and says the measure "creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate." It also says the state budget "has grown by 76% since 2018." Both the argument and its rebuttal say that within 24 hours of placing Prop 2 on the ballot, its backers voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits. The rebuttal adds that the measure "doesn't dedicate any new dollars" to education, health care or public safety. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
On the facts underneath: the enacted budget did suspend a $5.4 billion deposit, as described above. The LAO's analysis identifies no new spending; its only fiscal finding is that reserves would be higher. Rebates depend on revenue exceeding the limit over two years, which has not happened since 1986–87, and the state is $27.3 billion under the limit this year.
Proposition 2 leads 60% to 39% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 60% yes, 39% no and 1% undecided. Democrats back it 82% to 17% and independents 60% to 38%, while Republicans oppose it 77% to 22%. Renters support it 71% to 28% and homeowners 56% to 43%. One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies did not poll Prop 2 in September. PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom listed a yes on Prop 2 in the ballot slate he announced on October 9, and he and former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra are listed as supporters in the Voter Information Guide. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) opposes it. The Legislature's final votes were 29–2 in the Senate and 59–8 in the Assembly. Among editorial boards, the Sacramento Bee recommends yes and the San Diego Union-Tribune and the Orange County Register recommend no, according to CalMatters' voter guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/).
Proposition 2 after November 3 would take effect for the 2027–28 budget:
If Prop 2 passes, the new rules first apply to the budget the Governor proposes in January 2027 for the 2027–28 fiscal year. The cap on required savings rises to 20%, larger capital gains set-asides start in boom years, deposits stop counting against the spending limit until withdrawn, and required debt payments continue to 2040. The $15.1 billion now in the fund stays there, and nothing in the measure requires a deposit beyond the existing formulas. How fast the fund grows toward the new cap depends on revenue and on whether future budgets suspend deposits. If it fails, the 2014 rules stay in place, with the cap at 10% and required debt payments ending after 2029–30.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the text of ACA 20 (Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026), the 2026–27 enacted budget as described by the Legislative Analyst's Office on August 26, 2026, campaign-finance data as of October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State) and October 14, 2026 (FPPC), party and candidate positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–10, 2026.

The Billionaire Tax Takes A Dive
California’s proposed billionaire tax was supposed to win politically. Tax a few hundred extraordinarily wealthy people, raise billions for healthcare, and dare opponents to defend the billionaires.
Five days before Election Day, that proposition is looking considerably less attractive to voters.
A new Berkeley IGS Poll, released Thursday, finds Proposition 40 trailing by eight percentage points among likely voters. Fifty percent say they are voting No, compared with 42% voting Yes. Another 8% remain undecided.
Six weeks ago, the same poll had Proposition 40 ahead, 45% to 42%. That’s an eleven-point reversal, with opposition up eight points and support down three.
And the Berkeley poll isn’t the only one. A new Public Policy Institute of California survey also finds the measure trailing, 52% to 46%.
The significance extends beyond Proposition 40. Berkeley tested seven of the fourteen statewide ballot propositions, and just one currently commands majority support.
The survey was conducted October 19–25 among 1,477 likely voters, with an approximate sampling error of three percentage points.
But the most interesting story isn’t simply that a billionaire tax is losing support in one of America’s most Democratic states.
It’s what has happened to the campaign, who’s opposing it, and what the crosstabs reveal about California voters.
Bottom line: this measure is on a losing trajectory. But there’s a lot more to the story…

### Yes on Proposition 2
Increases State's Rainy Day Fund
#### What is it?
Prop 2 doubles the cap on California's rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
And it increases the amount the state saves when capital gains tax revenues are high.
Currently, California can only save up to 10% of the total budget (so if the State's budget were $300B, it could only legally save $30B).
Prop 2 would double the maximum savings cap.
California has hit the savings cap twice since it was created in 2014 as part of the Budget Stabilization Act that created the rainy day fund.
It would also save more capital gains tax revenue if capital gains account for more than 10% of the state's total tax revenue.

I'm checking which polls actually measured Prop 2: only PPIC, at 61-38 in October and 60-39 in September, so IGS didn't test it. The Indivisible El Dorado page cites an Aug 17 Berkeley IGS poll and some other figures, which I suspect are for Props 39 and 40 rather than Prop 2.

Yes still looks strongly favored, but I want to test that against ways it could fail. Voter fatigue with 14 measures and heavy anti-Prop 40 spending could drag down "Yes" generally, though Prop 2 isn't a tax. Opponents may frame it as a politicians' slush fund, yet no money seems to be pushing that message. Republicans and HJTA oppose it, and I'm running rough numbers on the electorate split to see whether Democrats would still carry it.

I'm now checking whether a 2024 Prop 6 poll exists, since a no-opposition legislative amendment failing would be a useful calibration case. I'm not sure PPIC or Berkeley IGS polled it, so I'll search to confirm.

I'm going back through past ballot measures to see how legislative amendments without organized opposition have fared, like the 2018 propositions, which mixed outcomes, and 2016's Prop 55, which passed comfortably.

I'm pulling up the calibration cases now: 2014's Prop 1 water bond passed at 67% and Prop 2 rainy day fund at 69%, and the 2009 May special's 1A failed at 35%, but that was an angry special election tied to a tax extension. Looking at the broader pattern, positively labeled legislative measures with no funded opposition have mostly passed, and rainy day funds in particular are popular. I also want to check whether PPIC's October 2024 poll had Prop 6 or any other ~60% measure that later failed, since that would be a useful caution.

I'm recalling which Prop 6 polls exist, and whether PPIC's October 2024 numbers covered it along with the other measures around 60%. I'm not sure of the exact figures, so I'll check them.

###### Quick Facts
- **Official ballot title:** “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.”
(Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026).

- **Type:** Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot).

- **A vote YES means:** California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues.
It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.

The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.

### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.

Who Are California's Infrequent Voters and When Do They ... https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/ For example, 81.63% of Californians were registered to vote ahead of the last governor's election in November 2022, yet only 50.08% of registered voters cast a ballot, according to the California Secretary of State. ... With such a wide gap between voter registration and participation, who are the voters who show up only occasionally? In PPIC Statewide Surveys, infrequent voters are registered voters who engage with politics less often and have less interest, as opposed to likely voters who are registered voters that indicate interest and engagement in politics. Infrequent voters are often younger, have lower incomes, are more racially diverse, and a plurality have a high school education or less. Although about half (51%) of infrequent voters identify as ideologically moderate (24% liberal, 25% conservative), about four in ten (42%) are Democrats (34% independents, 22% Republicans). Infrequent voters—similar to likely voters— are overall more likely to support Democratic candidates in the lead up to statewide elections and have shown similar levels of support for ballot propositions ahead of this year's gubernatorial election and in the 2025 special election. Final statistics from the Secretary of State indicate that Californians' overall turnout for presidential elections is higher than turnout for gubernatorial elections, and higher still compared to special elections. Despite these results, most infrequent voters in our surveys had said they intended to show up. Roughly e 2. How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

Committees are absent on both sides as of 10/22/2026, so the outcome will likely hinge on the ballot label, party endorsements, and slate mailers. The label "Increases State's Rainy Day Fund" reads as strongly positive, since low-information voters will probably associate it with saving for a rainy day rather than find it confusing. Next I'm weighing the "no default" heuristic.

I'm checking the PPIC's track record on past propositions: they overestimated Prop 5 in 2024 and underestimated Prop 6, so their errors run about 5 points either way. With the measure at 61% and roughly 11 points of room, the lead looks fairly safe even allowing for polling error.

I'm checking how accurate PPIC has been on past propositions, and it's been close: most results land within a few points of their final polls. Prop 2 at 61% with about 11 points of room looks like a likely pass. I'm now going to look at the October crosstabs by region, especially the Central Valley and Inland Empire.

Next I'm checking whether the 2024 school bond Prop 2 causes any confusion with this measure, though it likely doesn't matter much. I also want to see how the anti-Prop 40 billionaire money and its "Vote No on 40, Yes on 41/42" messaging interacts with Prop 2, since Prop 41 touches the spending limit and Prop 2 excludes reserve deposits from it.

I'm now checking whether Props 41 and 42 carry conflict language that would undo Prop 2 if they win more votes, though the real question is just which side wins on the Yes/No vote. I'll also look for any late news, like an October LA Times piece or a late opposition push, that could shift the picture.

Next I'm checking the LA Times voter guide on Prop 2 to see what the opposition arguments look like.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

Emerson apparently didn't poll Prop 2. The broader climate looks strongly Democratic, with Becerra ahead by roughly 24 to 27 points and Trump's approval in California around 26 to 33 percent, which tends to help Democratic-backed measures like Prop 2. I'm also going to check the California Today guide for ballot return data, since if Democrats are leading early returns that would be another point in Prop 2's favor.

I'm matching the income and education numbers to their groups by pairing the values so each set sums to the sample total. The first pair is renters and owners, then naturalized and native-born, then the three income brackets, and last the three education levels.

Education is last, with 69% for college graduates, 50% for those with some college, and 61% for high school only. Some college is the weakest group at 50%, and every other group is above that.

***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.

PROP 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

I've got enough to go on. Prop 2 on the November 3, 2026 ballot would grow the State's Rainy Day Fund through a legislative constitutional amendment that needs only a simple majority to pass. Both PPIC polls show it ahead, 60-39 in September and 61-38 in October, with a majority across every region and group, and I'm not finding any other polling. No funded campaign has registered on either side yet, and I'm now looking at who has come out in support, starting with Newsom.

I'm going through the rest of the support and opposition, including the editorial boards on each side. The prediction markets sit around 82% for Yes, and the historical comparisons and the Democratic-leaning midterm environment point the same way.

content.text:
yes

I'm confident in this. Results weren't posted when I checked (election night is November 3, 2026), so this is a forecast.

- **Polling:** The Public Policy Institute of California, the only pollster that asked about Prop 2, had it at 60% yes to 39% no in September and 61% to 38% in October. In October it had majority support in every region and every demographic group. Republicans were opposed, 23% yes, but Democrats were at 85% and independents at 57%. This pollster's October numbers have usually landed within about 5 points of the final result, so Prop 2 would need an unusually large late collapse to fail.
- **No real opposition campaign:** As of October 22, the Secretary of State listed no campaign committee for or against Prop 2. Opposition came from the Republican Party, Carl DeMaio's Reform California, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which called it a "Band-Aid," and a few editorial boards. None of them funded a "No" campaign, so most voters will mainly see the friendly ballot title, "Increases State's Rainy Day Fund."
- **Support:** Newsom, Becerra and the state Democratic Party back it, along with firefighters, hospitals, the LA Chamber of Commerce and the state PTA. The SF Chronicle, Mercury News and Sacramento Bee editorial boards endorsed it. The midterm looks Democratic-leaning, with Becerra up 24 to 27 points.
- **History:** Earlier rainy-day fund measures passed easily: 71% in 2004 and 69% in 2014.
- **Betting markets:** On November 2, Kalshi gave it a 92% chance of passing and Polymarket about 72%, though very little money was being traded.
